name: Vale
summary: A command-line linter for prose: it parses Markdown, AsciiDoc, HTML and code comments, then checks the text against style rules written as YAML files.
intro: Vale turns a writing style guide into checks that run in the editor and in CI. It ships almost no opinions of its own. A style is a folder of YAML rules, each built on one of 12 checks: `existence` flags listed words or patterns, `substitution` suggests a replacement, `capitalization` checks headings, `readability` scores a grade level with formulas such as Flesch-Kincaid and SMOG, `spelling` uses Hunspell dictionaries, and `script` runs custom logic. A `.vale.ini` file says which styles apply to which files, and `vale sync` downloads published packages such as Microsoft’s and Google’s style guides, proselint, write-good and alex.

What sets it apart is that it reads documents, not raw text. Markdown, AsciiDoc, reStructuredText, HTML and other formats go through a real parser, so a rule can target headings, lists or table cells, and code spans, URLs and fenced blocks are skipped. It lifts comments and docstrings out of source code with tree-sitter grammars, and “views” point it at the prose inside an OpenAPI file, a notebook or a commit message. It is a single Go binary that runs offline. Recent releases added rule inheritance, a standard library of rules (Std) and Voices, a package that turns the instructions people give LLMs about tone, such as “don’t hedge” or “no puffery”, into rules that check every draft.
strengths: Markup-aware: rules can target parts of a document, and code, URLs and front matter don’t raise false alarms
A house style becomes a folder of YAML files that anyone can read, review and extend, with no programming needed for most rules
One offline binary for macOS, Windows and Linux, so CI and editors need no Node.js or Python
A large ecosystem: published styles, a language server, a GitHub Action, and built-in use in docs platforms such as Mintlify
limits: Rules match words and patterns; Vale doesn’t understand meaning, so it can’t tell whether a sentence is correct or clear
Big word-list styles report many suggestions on existing docs until you tune levels, exceptions and vocabularies
Every project needs a `.vale.ini` and a `vale sync` step before the first run
Developed by one maintainer, funded by sponsors and grants

story: Earlier prose checkers such as proselint (Python) and write-good (Node.js) each needed their own language runtime and had little support for markup. Joseph Kato released Vale in February 2017 as a linter for prose “no matter if it’s plain text, markup or source-code comments”, written in Go and built around rules anyone could add. The 1.0 release in August 2018 bundled proselint, write-good and Joblint as styles, listing better markup support and a single binary as the reasons to use them through Vale.

Vale 2.0 (February 2020) took those bundled styles out into separate packages, so Vale itself carried only a minimal built-in style, and added XML and DITA support. Vale 3.0 (January 2024) added a default configuration and a shared `config` folder for dictionaries and vocabularies. The project, now under the vale-cli GitHub organisation, received a $10,000 FLOSS/fund grant in 2025, and in 2026 added rule inheritance, the Std library and Voices, aimed at checking text written by coding agents as well as people.

choices.choice: Parse markup instead of reading plain text
choices.why: Docs are written in Markdown, AsciiDoc or HTML full of code and links; parsing lets rules ignore code and target headings or other parts of a document.

choices.choice: Rules as YAML files, not code
choices.why: Editors and technical writers maintain style guides, so a rule had to be something they could write and review without programming.
Every organisation has its own style, so Vale ships the engine and leaves the rules to packages, which 2.0 split out of the binary.
Avoid the Node.js or Python install that write-good and proselint needed, so the same tool runs in any editor and CI.

timeline.text: August: 1.0, bundling proselint, write-good and Joblint styles
February: 2.0 moves styles into separate packages and adds XML
January: 3.0 adds a default config and a shared config folder
September: 3.20 adds rule inheritance, with the Std and Voices packages
